South African Comic Book Heroes

By: Julian Sun | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We showcase South Africa's burgeoning comic-book scene

Unique Selling Point:
Everybody dreams of doing something that they love for a living. In this story we showcase the amazing lives of several talented comic book artists whose dreams have become reality. In doing so, we reveal the passion that some South Africans have for comics and a burgeoning local comic book scene that seems to be going from strength to strength.

Summary:
From Batman to Superman, Wonder Woman, the Avengers and the Justice League, there are over 100 films and television shows either currently airing, scheduled for release, or in development. There’s no arguing that comic-book heroes are stars of modern pop culture. In South Africa, some very talented artists are making names for themselves both internationally and locally. In this story, we meet several of them. One plies his trade for Marvel Comics illustrating on characters like Deadpool, one has drawn Batman for D.C. Comics, a dynamic writing duo are the creators of the horror comic Survivor's Club, whilst another is the visionary behind the local comic-book character Kwezi.

Further information:
Our expose on the South African comic book scene we profile:

1. Sean Isaakse and his work on Marvel Comics. We’d interview him at his studio, see him at work and shoot very beautiful stylized shots of his process.

Sean will also assist with providing the name of somebody from Marvel Comics that we can interview about how Sean got the job at Marvel via Skype

2. I’ve also spoken with Jason Masters and he’s also agreed to participate. (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6ICQJtmWGKA) here’s a great link to an insert produced for Design Indaba a few years ago about his work. We’d take a similar approach when interviewing him and showcasing his work/process as Sean.

3. Loyiso Mkize - Loyiso is the main man behind a homegrown South African comic book black superhero Kwezi. This is a locally written, produced and distributed comic book. He will provide a nice counterpoint to the the guys doing work for DC & Marvel. We’d shoot them at their offices where we can meet the team behind Kwezi and look at the logistics behind producing a local comic book in SA (stuff like distribution, production, manufacturing etc)

http://10and5.com/2015/03/31/kwezi-a-south-african-superhero-comic/
http://kwezicomics.co.za/

4. Lauren Beukes &

To provide an expert opinion about the scene is a man called Moray Rhoda who is regarded as the authority about comic books in South Africa. http://www.designindaba.com/articles/point-view/secret-identity-sa-comics

We will shoot at the studios of Sean, Jason & Loyiso, as well as at a Johannesburg-based comic book shop like Smallville Comics in Alberton or Cosmic Comics in Randburg.

Press Release:


Comic-book heroes are stars of modern pop culture. Carte Blanche meets the brilliant South African illustrators bringing global superheroes to life as we spend time in the drawing rooms of those plying their trade for Marvel and D.C. Comics to the visionary behind local comic-book character, Kwezi.

Script:


INTRO V/O: Good Art is timeless, assuming a relevance to each new generation. It connects to the past and informs the future with a simple rigorous beauty that commands your gaze and thoughts. It could come from a still-life or a portrait. For many, it might even come from a comic book.

BONGANI: Spider-Man, Wonder Woman, The Justice League, there’s no denying how pervasive comic books have become as part of modern popular culture. And now a group of talented young South Africans are making their name in an industry that’s enjoying a 21st century boom.

V/O: Comic book and graphic novel sales reached over $1 billion in the US and Canada in 2015 and a small but passionate group of South African comic book artists are beginning to tap into this market.

It’s a community Moray Rhoda knows well. Considered to be the God Father of comics in South Africa, he explains why our artists are at last gaining international attention.

Moray: There are a lot more people interested in doing it because the potential for getting their stuff out has vastly improved over the past couple of years.

The Geek has inherited the Earth so where you’d be ostracized in the past for your liking of Sci-Fi and Fantasy and comic books and table-top gaming and video gaming, now it’s something that’s become relevant and I think our local artists are realizing that they can create their own audience.

V/O: For many an idealistic artist, the D.C or Marvel universe may seem like a world away but thanks to the internet, the idea of living locally and working globally is now possible. It’s allowed the talents of someone like Sean Isaakse to be recognized. He recently landed a dream job at Marvel Comics where he gets to draw his childhood heroes of his like Spider-Man and Thunderbolts.

Bongani: Sean, how did your love of comics begin?

Sean: When I was a kid, my mom and my dad were into comics. What really attracted me was like the colours from a really, really young age. My mom’s got pictures that I drew of like Spider-Man and Batman.

Bongani: So basically so as soon as you saw these things you wanted to draw them?

Sean: Ja, everything in life that I’ve done has just been to draw comic books, if I couldn’t be a super-hero myself, I wanted to draw them

V/O: Sean’s journey to success has taken years of dedication and perseverance with many false starts along the way until opportunity finally came knocking

Bongani: So what was your big break?

SEAN: What happened was I got retrenched from this design company I was working for. When I first got retrenched I started sending stuff to Marvel Comics. It was like a back and forth over the years, I’d send them new samples and then they’d send me critiques back.

V/O: After 6 years, Sean’s persistence finally paid off when he received an email from Marvel Comics.

Bongani: So what did it feel like to finally land this dream gig?

SEAN: When I got the e-mail saying “Marvel Work?”, I was like “Yeah no this is a joke”, someone’s sending this from a bum email or something. I was like this can’t be real and then when it dawned on me that it was an actual thing, it freaked me out.

You think to yourself that this is the dream you've wanted your whole life and now’s your shot, what if you can’t pull it off?

V/O: Another very talented illustrator is former graphic designer Jason Masters. For the past 5 years he’s drawn the likes of Batman for DC, The X-Men for Marvel and most recently, James Bond.

Bongani: Jason, it’s one thing to want something but how did you actually do it? How did you become a comic book illustrator?

Jason: There was a comic book shop called Cosmic Comics and they brought out quite a big name illustrator, an American artist called Ethan van Sciver. I was quite cheeky and I showed up with my portfolio. I was quite taken aback, he seemed to really like what I did. Months went by, probably 6 months and then I got an email from an editor at a company called Wild Storm who was part of D.C Comics at that point. “Hey Jason, we saw your work, thought it was quite good, would you like to try out and do some work?”

Bongani: What did that feel like?

Jason: It was both exciting and also terrifying, like is it enough, have I drawn enough? Is it good enough? You know you never know. If I do something for them, the whole world gets to see it and if I do a terrible job, that’s it. It’s kind of a terrifying moment.

Moray: It’s an incredibly big deal. I don’t people quite understand how difficult it is to get to that point and how hard these guys had to work, I know especially Jason, the stuff that he put out into the world had to be artwork that he was happy with.


Bongani: The life of a comic book artist can be a solitary one. Many long nights spent working in isolation behind a computer screen before one call realise all of this, but it’s a labour of love they wouldn’t have any other way

SEAN: You have to love it, you have to cos it’s a lot of work, it's a lot of sacrifice. You spend a lot of time cooped up at home or at your office drawing

BONGANI: What’s the longest you’ve spent working without seeing other people?

SEAN: Shew I think maybe 7 days, 7-8 days but at the same time I sit there and like at night, like 3 o Clock in the morning I'm busy drawing comic books and I’m like, “Holy Crap! I’m drawing Spider-Man!” officially, for a comic book!

V/O: It takes a collaborative effort to bring a comic book to life. On the one hand there are illustrators like Sean and Jason, on the other are writers like Lauren Beukes and Dale Halverson. This dynamic duo is the creative force behind the horror comic Survivors’ Club.

LAUREN: Novels will always be my first love because it’s the purest hit of story that you can get but comics is really fun and exciting and what I love about it is the sense of collaboration

DALE: When you’re writing a script and you realise that someone is has to draw this at some stage, so you have to always keep in mind that the things that you’re writing translate visually

LAUREN: That’s the magic of the collaboration is how the art informs the words and how it creates these shifts in you and kind of pushes the story in other directions you hadn’t anticipated.


V/O: Closer to home, there’s a growing audience of South African comic book fans hungry for new heroes they can identify with like Kwezi, written and drawn by Loyiso Mkize.

Loyiso: Kwezi is a passion project. I just wanted a character that looked like me, that spoke like me right? And then was around the same places that I was around.

MORAY: Loyiso has actually achieved the impossible: he’s taken the concept of a super-hero and he actually has placed it in our context.

LOYISO: Superhero’s like Kwezi will do a lot for children’s frame of reference. That informs how you behave because the character looks like you right? He speaks like you. We’re borrowing an entire art-form here right from the West. That’s fine, it’s the content that counts. Create characters that people can relate to, create narratives you know that people instinctively know and feel South African.

We went from printing a 100 copies back in 2014 and now we’re printing in excess of 6000 copies.

I want people to fall in love with the character, then we can have Marvel or DC collaborate with us and make big feature films, right, of Kwezi. Can you imagine? And that’s where I’m projecting it, I think that’s where the comic book is going!

V/O: This small community of South African comic book writers and illustrators are true pioneers, blazing a trail and giving hope to all aspiring artists, that their dreams might one day become reality.

BONGANI: What would your advice be to aspiring young artists and illustrators?

SEAN: Nothing’s out of reach, you know if you want it bad enough you can make it happen and sometimes you have to make some sacrifices but that’s when you need to just… Do you want it bad enough? And if you do nothing’s unattainable


V/O: The archetypal superhero is an ordinary person blessed with extraordinary powers, able to affect people all over the planet with their gift. If that’s the criteria, then this this current crop of talented artists and writers are indeed heroes themselves, inspiring a new generation of South Africans to follow in their footsteps. After all, with great power comes great responsibility.
